stories.title: Peter Schiff warns Bitcoin could fall below $16,500 if $50,000 breaks
stories.summary: Bitcoin critic Peter Schiff said Bitcoin could drop below $16,500 by year-end if it first falls through $50,000. Schiff is a longtime gold advocate known for bearish Bitcoin calls. The claim comes amid recent price weakness in the market.
stories.whyItMatters: Readers should weigh Schiff's long record of bearish Bitcoin predictions against actual price data, not treat this as a forecast.
questions: What specific evidence supports the $16,500 threshold?
How have Schiff's past Bitcoin predictions turned out?

sources.title: Peter Schiff argues Bitcoin may fall below $16,500 by year-end if $50,000 breaks next

stories.title: Bitcoin’s oil relief has a catch: more oil at sea, less on land
stories.summary: Bitcoin dropped below $64,000 over the weekend as leveraged bullish positions were liquidated. A related report linked part of the pullback to oil market shifts, noting more oil at sea and less on land. The move reverses recent price gains.
stories.whyItMatters: A drop through a key level with forced liquidations shows fragile trader positioning, which can add to volatility.
whatToWatch: Whether Bitcoin holds or breaks further below $64,000
Follow-up liquidation data from derivatives exchanges
questions: How much of the drop came from liquidations versus spot selling?
Is the oil-market link a real driver or a coincidence?

stories.title: Solana's 'retired' validators still vote with 15% of active stake
stories.summary: An analysis found that validators marked as retired on Solana still vote with about 15% of active stake. This raises questions about how Solana tracks validator status and reports decentralization.
stories.whyItMatters: Inaccurate validator status data can overstate how decentralized and secure the Solana network really is.
whatToWatch: Any response from Solana or validator operators
Changes to how retired status is tracked and reported
questions: Why do these validators still vote despite being labeled retired?
Does this change Solana's true decentralization figures?

sources.title: Solana’s “retired” validators still vote with 15% of active stake

stories.title: Forced Bitcoin Lightning channel exits can be cheap but slow
stories.summary: A report examined forced exits from Bitcoin's Lightning Network. Fees for these exits can be low, but users may still wait days before they can access their funds. The delay comes from how Lightning's on-chain dispute and settlement process works.
stories.whyItMatters: Lightning is marketed as a fast payments layer, so slow forced exits reveal a real tradeoff for users who need quick access to funds.
whatToWatch: Any proposed protocol changes to speed up forced exits
Lightning adoption trends given this tradeoff
questions: How often do forced exits happen in practice?
What exact step causes the multi-day wait?

sources.title: A forced Bitcoin Lightning exit can be cheap and still leave you waiting days

stories.title: Crypto industry spent $168 million on this election cycle, won 78 races
stories.summary: Crypto-aligned political spending reached $168 million in the latest election cycle, per CryptoSlate. Backed candidates won 78 races, including 13 newcomers, while one race brought a costly defeat for the industry.
stories.whyItMatters: Large political spending shows the industry is working to shape future crypto laws through direct electoral influence.
whatToWatch: How newly elected lawmakers vote on pending crypto bills
Whether spending rises further in future cycles
questions: Which race produced the costly defeat, and why?
How does this spending compare with other industries?

sources.title: Crypto’s $168 million election: 78 winners, 13 newcomers and one costly defeat

stories.title: Fake USDT can show a dollar balance in your wallet that you cannot sell
stories.summary: A report warned that spoofed USDT tokens can appear in a wallet with a dollar-denominated balance, even though the tokens cannot be sold or redeemed. These fake tokens are built to mimic Tether's real stablecoin.
stories.whyItMatters: Users who mistake fake tokens for real USDT risk believing they hold liquid value when they do not, a common scam pattern.
whatToWatch: Guidance from wallet providers or Tether on spotting fake tokens
Any enforcement action against issuers of spoofed tokens
questions: How are these fake tokens reaching victims' wallets?
Can wallets add automatic checks for spoofed stablecoins?

sources.title: Your wallet may show a dollar balance for fake USDT that you cannot sell

stories.title: Telegram curbs new in-chat apps after a no-tap hacking scare
stories.summary: Telegram has limited new in-chat mini apps after a security scare involving a no-tap hacking method, meaning the exploit needed no user interaction. The restriction affects developers who build apps inside Telegram, a platform widely used for crypto trading bots and communities.
stories.whyItMatters: Telegram hosts many crypto trading bots and wallets, so a platform-wide security clampdown can disrupt tools traders use daily.
whatToWatch: Which in-chat apps face restrictions and for how long
Further details from Telegram on the hacking method
questions: What exactly was exploited, and were users affected?
When will new app approvals resume?

sources.title: Telegram curbs new in-chat apps amid a no-tap hacking scare

stories.title: Evernorth's $35 million raise could buy 35 million XRP, but there's a catch
stories.summary: Evernorth raised $35 million in new funding. CryptoSlate notes the amount could theoretically buy 35 million XRP at current prices, but flags a catch around whether the funds will actually be used that way.
stories.whyItMatters: Large XRP-linked fundraising feeds into the broader trend of corporate treasuries adding crypto assets.
whatToWatch: Whether Evernorth confirms XRP purchases with the funds
More detail on the stated catch
questions: What exactly is the catch limiting the XRP purchase plan?
Who are Evernorth's investors, and what is its business model?

stories.title: MiCA gives crypto firms an EU passport, but customers still hit borders
stories.summary: The EU's MiCA regulation lets licensed crypto firms operate across member states under one authorization. A CryptoSlate report finds that despite this passporting system, customers still face border-like friction, such as uneven service availability across countries.
stories.whyItMatters: MiCA is the most complete crypto rulebook in a major market, so gaps between its intent and real enforcement affect how easily firms can scale across Europe.
whatToWatch: Regulatory guidance aimed at closing the cross-border gaps
Which member states lag in consistent MiCA enforcement
questions: What specific frictions are customers running into at borders?
Will EU regulators act to close these gaps?

sources.title: MiCA gave crypto a passport, but customers still face borders
